title: ARE WE GIVING SATAN THE ATTENTION THAT BELONGS TO JESUS?
paragraphs: ARE WE GIVING SATAN THE ATTENTION THAT BELONGS TO JESUS?
The Devil May Be Real, but He Is Not the Center of Your Story. And Some Christians Have Become So Busy Watching the Enemy That They Have Forgotten to Look at Their Savior.
What if one of the most dangerous distractions in your Christian life isn't something obviously sinful?
What if it's something that sounds spiritual, feels urgent, and even uses the language of warfare?
What if you've spent so much time talking about what Satan is doing that you've barely noticed what Jesus has already done?
Read that again.

Because somewhere between our prayers against the enemy, our warnings about demonic attacks, our fear of curses, and our endless conversations about spiritual warfare, a troubling question deserves an honest answer.
When did the defeated enemy become the main character in a story that was supposed to be about the victorious Christ?
And before you dismiss this as another article telling Christians to ignore spiritual warfare, stay with me.
Satan is real. Demonic opposition is real. Temptation is real. Spiritual warfare is biblical.
But so is the empty tomb.
And if our understanding of spiritual warfare leaves us more conscious of Satan's activity than Christ's authority, something has gone terribly wrong.
Because the Gospel was never meant to produce Christians who are constantly terrified of the devil.
It was meant to produce disciples who trust the risen Jesus.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable part of this conversation is that some of us have unintentionally made the enemy seem more powerful than the Savior we claim to worship.
Imagine a Christian woman sitting on the edge of her bed at two in the morning.

She has prayed. She has cried. She has listened to sermons about spiritual attacks. She has watched videos warning about hidden curses, generational strongholds, demonic doors, and the enemy's plans against her family.
Every disappointment has become an attack.
Every delay has become opposition.
Every nightmare has become a warning.
Every difficult relationship has become a battlefield.
She loves Jesus. She genuinely does.
But she is exhausted.
Not because Christ has abandoned her.
Not necessarily because a demon is attacking her.
But because she has learned to interpret almost everything through the possibility of Satan's involvement.
And somewhere along the way, her faith became a constant search for danger instead of a growing relationship with her Redeemer.
Perhaps you know someone like her.
Perhaps, painfully, you recognize yourself.
You wake up wondering what the enemy might do today instead of remembering whose mercy has carried you into another morning.
You spend more time investigating darkness than meditating on the light.
You can describe the enemy's strategies in astonishing detail, yet struggle to remember the promises of God when anxiety comes knocking.
You know how to rebuke.
But have you learned how to rest?
You know how to identify a battle.
But do you know how to abide in Christ?
You know the language of spiritual warfare.
But is your heart becoming more like Jesus?
Those questions are not meant to shame you.
They are meant to lead you back to the One who never stopped calling you closer.
Because Scripture does not command believers to become obsessed with Satan.
It commands us to be sober-minded, watchful, faithful, prayerful, and firmly rooted in Christ.
And there is an enormous difference.
The apostle Peter wrote:
“Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour: Whom resist stedfast in the faith.” — 1 Peter 5:8–9, KJV
Notice something remarkable.
Peter acknowledges the danger without making the danger the center of Christian existence.
He does not tell believers to spend their lives studying every movement of the devil.
He tells them to resist him, steadfast in the faith.
The Greek word translated “resist” is ἀντίστητε (antistēte), from a verb meaning to stand against or oppose.
It is a call to firm resistance, not frantic obsession.
And the phrase “steadfast in the faith” matters.
Our resistance is not rooted in how loudly we shout, how dramatically we pray, or how much secret knowledge we believe we possess about the kingdom of darkness.
It is rooted in faithful dependence upon God.
Peter's warning is serious.
But Peter's letter does not end with Satan.
It points suffering believers toward the God of all grace, who will restore, strengthen, and establish them (1 Peter 5:10).
Even when Peter talks about the devil, his destination is the faithfulness of God.
That should tell us something.
The enemy deserves vigilance. Jesus deserves worship.
Those are not the same thing.
And confusing them can quietly deform our spiritual lives.
Think about how Jesus Himself handled the temptation in the wilderness.
Matthew 4 tells us that the devil approached Jesus after forty days of fasting.
The temptations were deliberate.
Turn stones into bread.
Throw Yourself down and force a demonstration of divine protection.
Bow down and receive the kingdoms of the world.
Jesus did not respond by delivering a long speech about Satan's power.
He answered with Scripture.
“It is written.”
Again.
“It is written.”
And again.
“It is written.”
Then came the decisive command:
“Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve.” — Matthew 4:10, KJV
Jesus refused to let the tempter redefine His mission.
He would not exchange obedience for immediate satisfaction.
He would not turn trust into presumption.
He would not accept a crown by bowing before evil.
And the words He quoted came from Deuteronomy 6:13, where Israel was commanded to fear the LORD and serve Him.
In the Hebrew text, the phrase יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ תִּירָא וְאֹתוֹ תַעֲבֹד (YHWH elohekha tira ve'oto ta'avod) means, in context, “You shall fear the LORD your God, and Him you shall serve.”
The word tira comes from the Hebrew verb associated with fearing or revering.
This is not an invitation to live in terror of Satan.
It is a summons to give God the reverence and allegiance that belong to Him alone.
Jesus demonstrated the very priority that some believers are in danger of losing.
Worship belongs to God.
Obedience belongs to God.
Our deepest attention, ultimate allegiance, and lasting confidence belong to God.
Not to the enemy.
Not to the fear of the enemy.
Not even to our fascination with defeating the enemy.
To God.
And perhaps that is why some of the most powerful words Jesus ever spoke about spiritual authority were not the words many Christians emphasize.
In Luke 10, the seventy returned rejoicing that demons were subject to them through Jesus' name.
Imagine their excitement.
They had witnessed something extraordinary.
They had seen the authority of Christ demonstrated in their ministry.
Jesus affirmed the reality of that authority.
But then He redirected their joy.
“Notwithstanding in this rejoice not, that the spirits are subject unto you; but rather rejoice, because your names are written in heaven.” — Luke 10:20, KJV
Let those words settle into your heart.
Jesus did not deny the significance of spiritual authority.
He taught His disciples that something greater deserved their joy.
Their relationship with God.
Their place in His saving purposes.
The grace that had brought them into His kingdom.
The miracle was not merely that demons submitted to them.
The greater reason for rejoicing was that they belonged to God.
And this raises a question worth sitting with.
If Jesus told His disciples not to make authority over demons their greatest reason for rejoicing, why have some of us made demonic activity the subject of nearly every spiritual conversation?
We talk about attacks.
We talk about curses.
We talk about enemies.
We talk about hidden forces.
But how often do we talk about the holiness of God?
The beauty of repentance?
The cost of the cross?
The wonder of forgiveness?
The transforming work of the Holy Spirit?
The quiet miracle of a hardened heart becoming tender again?
The beauty of a father apologizing to his children?
The courage of a wife choosing truth instead of pretending her marriage is healthy?
The repentance of a man who finally confesses the sin he has hidden for years?
The grace of Jesus meeting someone in the ruins of decisions they can never undo?
These are not small things.
These are places where the Gospel changes actual human lives.
And sometimes, while we are searching for dramatic evidence of the enemy, we overlook the ordinary, costly, beautiful work of Christ.
A man loses his temper and wounds his family.
Instead of admitting that he has allowed anger to govern his words, he says the enemy attacked his home.
A woman becomes consumed by jealousy.
Instead of confessing envy and learning contentment, she assumes someone has placed a spiritual curse upon her happiness.
A believer refuses to forgive.
Instead of confronting bitterness, he spends months praying against every perceived enemy.
Now, spiritual opposition can be real.
But Scripture never teaches us to attribute every sinful choice, painful circumstance, or personal failure directly to Satan.
James writes:
That verse should sober us.
Sometimes the problem is not a demon hiding behind the door.
Sometimes it is pride sitting openly in the heart.
Sometimes it is greed.
Sometimes it is unforgiveness.
Sometimes it is an appetite we refuse to discipline.
Sometimes it is a lie we keep telling ourselves because the truth would require repentance.
And blaming Satan for everything can become a convenient way of avoiding the responsibility God calls us to embrace.
It is easier to say, “The enemy is attacking my marriage,” than to admit, “I have been selfish, dishonest, or cruel.”
It is easier to say, “The devil is stealing my peace,” than to examine whether we have been feeding our minds with fear and refusing to bring our anxieties to God.
It is easier to search for an invisible enemy than to confront a visible pattern of disobedience.
But Jesus did not come merely to help us identify evil outside ourselves.
He came to save sinners.
To forgive us.
To cleanse us.
To give us new hearts.
To call us away from darkness and into His marvelous light.
And genuine spiritual maturity requires us to recognize both the reality of external temptation and the responsibility of personal repentance.
That is not condemnation.
That is grace telling the truth.
Because the Savior who exposes sin is also the Savior who offers forgiveness.
Consider the man in Mark 5 who lived among the tombs.
His life had become a portrait of torment.
He cried out.
He wounded himself.
He lived isolated among the dead.
The Gospel account describes him as possessed by unclean spirits.
People tried to restrain him with chains, but they could not restore him.
Then Jesus arrived.
And the story changed.
The demons were real.
Their destructive influence was real.
The man's suffering was real.
But the central revelation of that encounter was not the greatness of the demonic powers.
It was the authority and compassion of Jesus Christ.
The man who had lived among the tombs was later seen sitting, clothed, and in his right mind.
And when he wanted to accompany Jesus, the Lord gave him an astonishing assignment.
“Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee.” — Mark 5:19, KJV
Do you see it?
Jesus did not commission him to build his identity around the demons that once tormented him.
He told him to testify about the mercy he had received.
Not, “Go and make everyone fascinated by your darkness.”
But, “Tell them what the Lord has done for you.”
The man had a history of torment.
But his future would be marked by testimony.
His past was not denied.
It was no longer the center of his identity.
And somebody reading this needs to hear that.
You may have a past filled with shame.
You may have been trapped in addictions, destructive relationships, bitterness, sexual sin, spiritual confusion, or years of rebellion.
You may have spent so long describing what went wrong that you have forgotten to celebrate what Christ is making new.
But if you belong to Jesus, your deepest identity is not your worst chapter.
Your story is not ultimately about the darkness that held you.
It is about the Redeemer who came for you.
From scandal to grace. Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling sin harmless.
Not by removing the need for repentance or accountability.
But by meeting guilty and broken people with a mercy that neither excuses evil nor abandons the sinner who turns to Him.
That is the scandalous beauty of grace.
Jesus does not merely change the language of our story.
He changes its direction.
And nowhere is that truth clearer than at the cross.
Colossians 2:13–15 describes God's saving work in Christ.
Paul speaks of forgiveness, the cancellation of the record of debt against us, and Christ's triumph over hostile spiritual powers.
Verse 15 declares:
“And having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it.” — Colossians 2:15, KJV
The Greek verb ἀπεκδυσάμενος (apekdysamenos) is commonly understood here in the sense of stripping off or disarming.
The language of triumph presents Christ's decisive victory over hostile powers.
Scholars discuss certain details of the Greek construction, but Paul's central emphasis is unmistakable: the crucified Christ is victorious.
The cross was not Satan's ultimate success.
It was the place where God accomplished redemption through His Son.
What looked like humiliation became the revelation of divine wisdom and saving power.
What looked like defeat was followed by resurrection.
And the enemy who seeks to accuse God's people does not possess the final verdict over those who are in Christ.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — KJV
That does not mean Christians will never experience temptation, suffering, accusation, or spiritual conflict.
It means that condemnation does not have the final word over those united to Christ.
Jesus does.
So why do we sometimes speak as though the devil has more authority over a redeemed believer than the Savior who purchased that believer with His blood?
Why do we act as though every setback proves Satan is winning?
Why do we sometimes live as though the cross is merely a symbol of hope rather than the decisive saving act of God?
Perhaps because fear is loud.
And faith often grows in quiet places.
Fear demands immediate attention.
Faith learns to trust what God has said even when emotions are unsettled.
Fear makes us desperate to know every possible threat.
Faith teaches us to know the Shepherd's voice.
Fear keeps asking, “What if Satan attacks?”
Faith asks, “How can I remain faithful to Jesus whatever comes?”
And there is something profoundly freeing about that change of focus.
Not because we suddenly become invulnerable.
Not because suffering disappears.
But because our security is no longer built upon our ability to predict or control every danger.
It rests upon the character and promises of God.
This is why James 4:7 is so important.
“Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” — KJV
Notice the order.
Submit to God.
Resist the devil.
The Greek word ὑποτάγητε (hypotagēte) means “submit” or “place yourselves under” authority.
And ἀντίστητε (antistēte), again, means “resist” or “stand against.”
The command begins with our relationship to God.
It does not begin with fascination about Satan.
Submission is not a decorative introduction to spiritual warfare.
It is essential to the Christian life.
You cannot substitute dramatic declarations against darkness for ordinary obedience to God.
You cannot nurture secret sin all week and assume a few shouted words will replace genuine repentance.
You cannot continually reject the teachings of Jesus and expect spiritual maturity to emerge from religious intensity alone.
James is addressing a community troubled by worldliness, conflict, and divided loyalties.
His call is not merely to confront the devil.
It is to draw near to God, cleanse their hands, purify their hearts, humble themselves, and repent.
And that is where some of us need to return.
Not to another endless search for hidden enemies.
But to honest surrender.
To prayer without performance.
To Scripture without sensationalism.
To worship without fear-driven obsession.
To repentance without excuses.
To the daily, sometimes difficult work of following Jesus.
Paul teaches spiritual warfare in Ephesians 6.
He tells believers to put on the whole armor of God.
He speaks of the devil's schemes and of spiritual forces of evil.
He does not minimize the battle.
But look at the armor.
Truth.
Righteousness.
The readiness that comes from the Gospel of peace.
Faith.
Salvation.
The Word of God.
Prayer.
This is not a costume for spiritual theatrics.
It is a picture of believers standing firm through God's provision.
And the passage begins with a command that should never be forgotten:
“Be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might.” — Ephesians 6:10, KJV
Not strong in your ability to frighten demons.
Not strong in your knowledge of occult terminology.
Not strong in your confidence that you can identify every spiritual attack.
Strong in the Lord.
The Greek expression ἐνδυναμοῦσθε ἐν κυρίῳ (endynamousthe en kyriō) communicates being strengthened in the Lord.
The source of strength is not the believer's independent power.
It is the Lord Himself.
And that changes everything.
Because Christian courage is not pretending that evil is powerless in every present circumstance.
It is trusting that evil does not possess ultimate authority over Christ.
The New Testament still warns believers against the devil.
It still commands resistance.
It still speaks of spiritual conflict.
But it never invites us to build a Christian identity around fear of darkness.
Our life is hidden with Christ in God (Colossians 3:3).
Our minds are to be set on things above (Colossians 3:1–2).
Our eyes are to be fixed upon Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith (Hebrews 12:2).
The Greek expression in Hebrews 12:2 begins with ἀφορῶντες εἰς Ἰησοῦν (aphorōntes eis Iēsoun).
It conveys the idea of looking toward Jesus with focused attention.
That is a beautiful picture of Christian perseverance.
The surrounding passage describes believers running the race set before them, laying aside sin and every hindrance, and enduring through hardship.
Where are their eyes directed?
Toward Jesus.
Not because the obstacles are imaginary.
Not because suffering is unimportant.
But because the One who endured the cross and is seated at God's right hand is worthy of their unwavering trust.
And maybe that is the correction our generation needs.
We have become skilled at spotting darkness.
But are we becoming skilled at recognizing Christlike character?
We can spend hours debating demonic influences.
But can we spend ten minutes confessing our own pride?
We can identify spiritual warfare in everyone else's life.
But can we admit when our own words have wounded someone?
We can declare that Satan is defeated.
But do we live as though Jesus is Lord?
That last question is the one that reaches beneath the surface.
Because saying “Jesus is Lord” is more than making a religious statement.
It is a confession that calls for allegiance.
The Greek phrase Κύριος Ἰησοῦς (Kyrios Iēsous) means “Jesus is Lord.”
It is central to the New Testament's proclamation of Christ's authority.
And if He is Lord, then He has authority over our decisions.
Our relationships.
Our hidden habits.
Our money.
Our words.
Our ambitions.
Our fears.
Our worship.
Our treatment of people who cannot benefit us.
Our willingness to forgive.
Our response when nobody is watching.
The enemy may tempt us.
But Jesus calls us to follow Him.
And following Him is where faith becomes more than religious vocabulary.
It becomes a transformed life.
There is a particularly sobering warning in Acts 19.
Some itinerant Jewish exorcists attempted to invoke the name of Jesus over an evil spirit, using the authority associated with the Jesus whom Paul preached.
But the encounter exposed the danger of treating Jesus' name as a formula detached from genuine submission to Him.
The episode ended in humiliation and fear.
And the larger narrative resulted in the name of the Lord Jesus being magnified, with people confessing their practices and turning away from magic.
The point is not that Christians must discover a more powerful verbal technique.
It is that Jesus is not a magical instrument to be used for personal control.
He is Lord.
And no religious phrase can replace a real relationship of faith and obedience.
Some people want the authority associated with Jesus without surrendering to Jesus.
They want victory without repentance.
Power without holiness.
Deliverance without discipleship.
The benefits of the kingdom without the King.
But Christ never offered Himself as an accessory to our existing lives.
He calls us to deny ourselves, take up our cross, and follow Him.
And that call is far deeper than a moment of emotional excitement.
It is a lifetime of grace-fueled transformation.
Perhaps you are reading this after years of living under spiritual fear.
Maybe you have been taught that every family difficulty is a curse.
That every illness is demonic.
That every financial struggle is evidence of an attack.
That every anxious thought means the enemy has gained control.
Please hear this carefully.
Scripture does not authorize us to make those assumptions.
The Bible recognizes spiritual evil, but it also recognizes sickness, human weakness, ordinary suffering, injustice, consequences of human choices, and the brokenness of creation.
Jesus Himself rejected a simplistic connection between personal sin and a man's blindness in John 9:1–3.
And when Elijah was exhausted and overwhelmed in 1 Kings 19, God's care included rest, food, and gentle direction.
Not every hardship has a single explanation.
Not every struggle requires a dramatic spiritual diagnosis.
Sometimes you need to repent.
Sometimes you need to forgive.
Sometimes you need wise counsel.
Sometimes you need rest.
Sometimes you need medical care.
Sometimes you need help from mature believers who will walk with you in truth and love.
And in every circumstance, you need the grace and wisdom of God.
There is no shame in receiving appropriate help.
Faithfulness does not require us to deny the ordinary means through which God can care for people.
The Lord who made us knows that we are dust.
He is not glorified by our pretending to be stronger than we are.
He is glorified when we trust Him enough to walk in truth.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking consequence of excessive attention to Satan is not simply that it produces fear.
It is that it can steal our attention from the beauty of Jesus.
We become so concerned with what the enemy might be doing that we fail to marvel at what the Savior has done.
The Son of God entered our broken world.
He welcomed sinners.
He touched lepers.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He fed the hungry.
He wept beside a tomb.
He forgave those who came to Him in repentance and faith.
He gave His life as a ransom for many.
He rose from the dead.
And He calls us into a new life shaped by His love and truth.
There is enough glory in Christ to occupy the Christian heart for a lifetime.
Yet sometimes we give more emotional energy to a frightening story about demons than to the resurrection of Jesus.
More attention to alleged curses than to the promises of God.
More fascination to the enemy's supposed plans than to the mission Christ entrusted to His Church.
And somewhere in the noise, the simple invitation of Jesus waits to be heard again.
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28, KJV
He did not say, “Come to Me only after you have identified every hidden attack.”
He did not say, “Come to Me when you have mastered every spiritual warfare formula.”
He said, “Come unto me.”
To Him.
The Person.
The Savior.
The Lord.
The One who knows every secret and still calls sinners to repentance and grace.
And maybe tonight, that is the invitation your soul has been waiting for.
Not another terrifying warning.
Not another explanation of why your life feels like a battlefield.
But a return to Jesus Himself.
The Jesus who is holy enough to confront your sin and merciful enough to forgive it.
The Jesus who will not flatter your pride but will receive the humble.
The Jesus who does not promise a painless life but promises His presence with His people.
The Jesus who can be trusted even when you do not understand what is happening around you.
You do not have to understand every strategy of the enemy to obey the Word of God.
You do not have to identify every spiritual force to pray with confidence in your Father.
You do not have to turn every disappointment into a supernatural conspiracy to believe that God is sovereign.
You can acknowledge the reality of spiritual warfare without making Satan the center of your spiritual imagination.
You can be watchful without becoming consumed by suspicion.
You can resist evil without living in terror.
You can take sin seriously without despairing of grace.
And you can pursue holiness without losing the joy of salvation.
Because the Christian life is not ultimately about becoming an expert on the devil.
It is about knowing, loving, trusting, obeying, and becoming more like Jesus Christ.
So perhaps the prayer we need tonight is not the loudest prayer we have ever prayed.
Perhaps it is the most honest.

“Lord Jesus, forgive me for the times I have allowed fear to become louder than Your promises. Forgive me for giving darkness more attention than Your Word. Teach me to resist evil without becoming obsessed with it. Expose the sins I have excused. Heal what is wounded in me. Give me discernment without suspicion, courage without pride, and peace rooted in Your truth. Let my life be known not for how much I talk about Satan, but for how faithfully I follow You. Amen.”
And if that prayer uncovered something you have been carrying, do not bury the moment beneath another scroll.
Let it become a turning point.
Maybe you have been afraid for so long that you have forgotten what it feels like to pray with confidence in God's love.
Maybe you have blamed the enemy for choices that require your repentance.
Maybe you have spent years fighting battles in your imagination while neglecting the simple obedience Christ has placed before you.
Maybe your faith has become loud on the outside but weary on the inside.
You are invited to come back.
Not to a shallow version of Christianity that ignores evil.
But to a Christ-centered faith that puts evil in its proper place.
A faith where the devil is resisted, sin is confessed, truth is loved, Scripture is treasured, the Church is strengthened, and Jesus is worshiped above all.
Or, if you have been spiritually exhausted and need prayer, simply comment, “Pray for me.”
You do not have to disclose private struggles to strangers. A few honest words can be enough to invite encouragement from brothers and sisters in Christ.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to manufacture fear.
Not to make believers dependent on dramatic spiritual content.
Not to build a community around fascination with darkness.
But to keep pointing people toward the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
Toward Scripture.
Toward repentance and grace.
Toward biblical discipleship.
Toward a faith that does not disappear when emotions settle.
And if this message helped you see Jesus more clearly, would you consider helping it reach someone else?
Someone may be exhausted from treating every difficulty as an attack.
Someone may be longing for a Christianity that is both spiritually serious and deeply rooted in the peace of Christ.

Invite your family, your friends, believers who have grown weary, people who are seeking truth, and even those who are unsure what they believe. They do not have to pretend to have everything figured out to begin hearing the Gospel.
There is another way you can help this ministry continue.
Scripture teaches that supporting Gospel ministry can be a meaningful expression of generosity and partnership.
Paul wrote:
“For we are labourers together with God.” — 1 Corinthians 3:9, KJV
But the broader New Testament does affirm voluntary, generous support for Gospel ministry.
In Philippians 4:15–18, Paul thanks believers for sharing in his ministry through their gifts.
And 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should be willing, not pressured:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
That distinction matters.
Your standing before God rests upon His grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not a monthly payment.

You may choose to include it in your personal budget for ministry giving, alongside your commitments to your local church and other responsibilities. Whether you regard such support as an offering is a matter to consider prayerfully within your own Christian convictions; it should not automatically replace the giving and stewardship responsibilities you have already embraced.
These items are not the reason we proclaim Christ.
They are simply another way to encourage faith, share biblical messages, and support the ongoing work.
That free library reflects something important about the heart of this mission.
The Gospel is not for sale.
And those who are unable to give financially can still make a meaningful difference by praying, sharing biblical teaching, encouraging others, and inviting people to grow in the Word of God.
Give freely if you choose to give.
Share faithfully if you choose to share.
And above everything, glorify Jesus in the way you live.
Because the goal is not to build an audience that admires a ministry.
The goal is to serve people who will love and follow Christ.
And that brings us back to the question that began this entire conversation.
Are Christians giving Satan too much attention and Jesus too little?
Sometimes, yes.
Not every Christian.
Not every discussion of spiritual warfare.
Not every warning about the enemy.
But whenever fear of Satan becomes more prominent in our hearts than confidence in Christ, we need to return to the biblical center.
Whenever our conversations about demons outnumber our conversations about discipleship, we should examine our priorities.
Whenever we become more excited about spiritual confrontation than about repentance, love, holiness, and the Gospel, we should ask what is shaping our imagination.
And whenever we make Satan seem like the controlling force in our story, we need to remember the authority of the risen Lord.
Jesus said:
“All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth.” — Matthew 28:18, KJV
The Greek text uses πᾶσα ἐξουσία (pasa exousia), meaning “all authority.”
That is the authority from which the Great Commission flows.
Jesus did not announce His authority so that His followers would spend their lives obsessing over Satan.
He sent them to make disciples of all nations, baptizing and teaching people to obey everything He had commanded.
And He promised to be with them.
That is our mission.
Not endless speculation about darkness.
But faithful witness to the Light.
Not making the devil famous.
But proclaiming Jesus Christ.
Not denying the battle.
But remembering who holds ultimate authority.
One day, the final defeat of Satan and evil will be fully manifested, as Revelation 20:10 declares.
Until then, believers remain called to vigilance, endurance, faith, and obedience.
We do not pretend the battle has disappeared.
We simply refuse to make the enemy the object of our devotion.
Because the cross is not a footnote in Satan's story.
Satan is a defeated enemy in the larger story of God's redeeming purpose through Jesus Christ.
And if you have spent years looking over your shoulder in fear, perhaps today is the day to look again toward your Savior.
Open the Scriptures.
Return to prayer.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Seek help where help is needed.
Forgive where forgiveness is required.
Stand firm in the faith.
Love your neighbor.
Serve your church.
Tell someone what Jesus has done for you.
And when the enemy comes to mind, do not allow fear to become the center of your worship.
Remember the One who died.
Remember the One who rose.
Remember the One who reigns.
Remember the One who is coming again.
And let your life become a testimony not to the greatness of the darkness you once feared, but to the greater glory of the Savior who called you into His light.
Because the most tragic thing would not be that you spent your life knowing the enemy was real, but that you became so consumed with the enemy that you neglected to know your Savior more deeply.
